title: Invention is Drudgery: why great things take unglamorous, relentless trial and error
summary: Jason Cohen argues that every creation, from Edison's light bulb to a band's gig, rests on enormous hidden drudgery. We see only the finished result, so we feel bad about being mid-journey, and quit. Those who succeed are the ones who plodded through the failures.

principles.text: Success is built on hidden drudgery; we only see the visible glory, so we underestimate the work required.
principles.quote: In the audience, we enjoy the show, blind to the hundred hours of toil behind each visible hour of glory.

principles.text: Don't compare your Chapter Four to someone else's last page; everyone has to take the whole journey.
principles.quote: Having skipped to the last page of other peoples' book, we forget that they took the journey of the whole book.

principles.text: Creating something great demands trial and error through thousands of failures, not a single flash of invention.
principles.quote: But the ones who eventually succeed are the ones who plodded through the 5,999 filaments that didn't work, put in the 10,000 hours master a craft, and fought through the overwhelming pile of challenges and drudgery that is always required to create something great.

principles.text: Products have no clear finish line like a book, which makes it hard to know whether to persist or quit.
principles.quote: A book has a clear end; products don't. It's often unclear whether it's smarter to continue or to quit.

principles.text: Quitting is tempting because the grind is real; the next job or startup won't be free of drudgery either.
principles.quote: We quit the job thinking wrongly that the next company will be so much better.

principles.text: Outsiders will dismiss hard-won success as luck, and they are not entirely wrong; do it for the meaning of accomplishment.
principles.quote: And that's the cue for others to dismiss it as mostly luck. The most annoying part is: They're not altogether wrong.
